country_overview: The United States Federal Reserve System (the Federal Reserve) is the central bank and sets monetary policy, while U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) administer cross-border currency reporting. The United States has a free-floating exchange-rate arrangement; under IMF Article VIII it maintains an exchange system free of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions (the US dollar is freely convertible, with no multiple currency practices), except for restrictions maintained solely for security reasons. Capital-account movements are separately regulated. The US dollar is the world's primary reserve currency.

summary.traveler: Travelers may carry unlimited US dollars or foreign currency, but any person transporting more than USD 10,000 in aggregate — cash or monetary instruments — into or out of the United States must file a Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) with CBP at the border. Amounts of USD 10,000 or less require no declaration.
summary.business: For current international transactions, businesses and individuals can make and receive payments and transfers without exchange restrictions under the United States' IMF Article VIII status, except for measures maintained solely for security reasons. Foreign-currency account access, repatriation, and capital-account movements are governed separately and remain an open evidence gap pending the US OECD reservation schedule.

rules.bring_foreign_currency_in: Foreign currency and US dollars may be imported without limit or prohibition. Any person bringing more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) into the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with a CBP officer at the port of entry.
rules.take_foreign_currency_out: US dollars and foreign currency may be exported without limit. Any person taking more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) out of the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with CBP before departure; non-residents may freely re-export funds they lawfully brought in.
rules.cash_declaration_threshold: The reporting threshold is USD 10,000. Under 31 U.S.C. 5316 and 31 CFR 1010.340, transporting an aggregate amount exceeding that figure across the US border triggers a mandatory Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) to CBP. This traveler border report is distinct from Bank Secrecy Act filings by financial institutions — Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — and from Foreign Bank Account Reports (FBAR); none of those is a traveler declaration.
rules.resident_holding_rules: Whether US residents may hold or maintain foreign-currency accounts without a general prior-approval regime is a capital-account / account-access question that the IMF Article VIII current-account finding does not settle. It is recorded as an open evidence gap pending the US reservation schedule under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements; account access is subject to sanctions, AML/KYC, tax, and prudential requirements.
rules.non_resident_rules: For non-residents, whether accounts may be opened and funds transferred without a general prior-approval regime is likewise a capital-account / account-access matter not settled by the IMF Article VIII current-account finding, and is recorded as an open evidence gap pending the US OECD reservation schedule. Onboarding is subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, information-reporting and withholding, and institution requirements.
rules.business_invoicing_settlement: Business transactions may be invoiced and settled in US dollars or foreign currency. For current international transactions, cross-border commercial payments are free of exchange restrictions under the United States' IMF Article VIII status, subject to sanctions, AML reporting, and tax requirements; capital-account elements are governed separately and are not established by that finding.
rules.exchange_controls: The United States has a free-floating exchange-rate arrangement and, having accepted IMF Article VIII, maintains an exchange system free of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions, with no multiple currency practices — except for restrictions maintained solely for the preservation of national or international security, notified to the IMF. This finding covers current international transactions; capital-account movements are governed separately under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements and the US reservation schedule.
rules.banking_conversion_practicality: In practice, foreign-exchange conversion and transfers are widely offered by US banks, licensed money-services businesses, and ATMs. This is a practical-availability observation that has not been tied to a claim-specific official source, so it is recorded as an open evidence gap; access is subject to each institution's AML/KYC and sanctions-screening procedures.

disclaimer: This page provides general informational reference only. Foreign-exchange rules in the United States are subject to change, and transaction-specific requirements may depend on residency status, documentation, amount, and the applicable Federal Reserve / CBP / FinCEN framework. This is not legal, regulatory, tax, financial, or compliance advice.
